claims.text: Slight controlled compositional modifications in alternating CoCrFeMnNi layers will produce quantifiable lattice-parameter differences.
Alternating layers with different lattice parameters will create high-density coherent interfaces.
The engineered coherent interfaces will act as strong barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will enhance resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Lattice-parameter variations will force dislocation pile-ups at coherent interfaces.
Dislocation pile-ups at coherent interfaces increase the energy barrier for dislocation transmission.
An increased barrier to dislocation transmission delays the onset of creep.
Engineered lattice-mismatched multilayers will exhibit lower creep displacement than the homogeneous baseline.
Engineered lattice-mismatched multilayers will exhibit a higher creep stress exponent than the homogeneous baseline.
Pronounced interfacial dislocation pile-ups will correlate with improved creep resistance.
TEM can be used to detect the proposed dislocation pile-ups at interfaces.
XRD and modeling can verify the engineered lattice-parameter differences.
The mechanism is expected to operate for layer thicknesses between 10 and 100 nm.
The mechanism is expected to operate from room temperature to approximately 600 K.
Maintaining the stated thickness and temperature ranges will ensure that the coherent interfaces remain stable.
At temperatures or layer thicknesses beyond the stated ranges, other deformation mechanisms or phase instabilities may dominate.
Residual stresses, microstructural inhomogeneities, and imperfect lattice-parameter control may affect the magnitude of creep improvement.
